message.content: {"summary":"You built a clear, well-ordered report that lands on a justified not-ship conclusion, with sensible stakeholder mapping and EACE links. The main gaps are evidential: the for-shipping side rests on assertion rather than sources, one citation does not support the claim it carries, and several references are incomplete. You also stop short of saying when shipping might be acceptable and of tailoring decision guidance to individual stakeholders.","next_steps":["Rebuild the evidence base in DICUSSION: replace the CNBC claim about outpacing Samsung and Google with a source that actually says it, add external support for the commercial/competitive argument, and give at least one quantitative figure (e.g. recall or outage cost data from the NHS or Volkswagen cases) so the analysis is not purely qualitative.","In The Most Ethical Path, add a short section setting out the conditions under which shipping could be defensible (documented risk assessment, disclosure of the known defect to affected clients, agreed mitigation and monitoring), and check each EACE clause you cite against the code text so 2.1b, 2.3b and 3.3 are used for what they actually say.","Reach the Excellent descriptors by making the argument systematic across stakeholders: state what Rachel, her manager, the chip contractor and the health department should each do and why, add a decision flowchart or stakeholder impact table, and proofread the headings and sentences before submission."],"criteria":{"C1":"You identify end-user harm, professional responsibility and reputational risk and link them to engineering design, and you name the stakeholders explicitly. To reach Excellent, move beyond the generic 'rapidly growing industry' remark and discuss the organisational context directly: shipping deadlines, pressure from management, the absence or presence of formal ethics review, and how those forces shape Rachel's judgement.","C2":"Arguments for and against shipping are developed and lead to a clear position. The for-shipping claims are asserted rather than evidenced, and you never say when shipping would be acceptable. Add the conditions under which release could be justified, support the competitive-advantage argument with evidence, and give each stakeholder group separate decision guidance rather than one collective recommendation.","C3":"Your structure moves from discussion to weighing to conclusion to recommendations, and the conclusion follows from what you argued. The for-shipping case is answered only briefly and the reasoning is uneven across stakeholders. To reach Excellent, work through each stakeholder's position systematically and show explicitly how each recommendation traces back to a specific argument in DICUSSION.","C4":"The EACE code, the BBC NHS report and the Volkswagen case are relevant and well chosen. The CNBC source does not support the Samsung and Google claim, and the for-shipping side has no external support at all. Broaden the reference base, add quantitative evidence, and fix references [1], [3] and [4] so all entries carry a full author, title and working URL in one consistent style.","C5":"All required sections are present and the report reads clearly, but there are no figures or tables and accuracy needs a careful proofread. To reach Excellent, add visual elements that carry argument weight, such as a stakeholder impact table or a ship/no-ship decision flowchart, and apply one referencing style consistently across the whole reference list."}}
